items.title: L11: Writing a submission to a minister
items.source: Civil Service Code; Cabinet Office guidance on working with ministers' private offices; Civil Service Success Profiles (Communicating and Influencing)
items.body: A submission is written advice from officials to a minister, normally sent through the minister's private office. Private secretaries are civil servants: they manage the minister's papers and diary, pass on decisions and are bound by the Civil Service Code like any other official. A good submission usually opens with the purpose, the decision needed and the deadline. Background follows, kept short. The core is a set of options with the advantages and disadvantages of each, then a clear recommendation. Further sections cover risks, financial and legal implications, how the decision will be announced or handled in Parliament and the media, and who has been consulted. Finance, legal and communications colleagues often clear the relevant sections before it goes up, and the author and clearing officials are responsible for the facts being accurate. Advice must be honest and complete even when the minister is unlikely to welcome it. The minister decides; officials then carry out the decision. Decisions should come back in writing, usually through the private office, so there is a record of what was decided and why. If a minister later changes an instruction by phone or in a meeting, officials normally ask for it to be confirmed in writing and note it on the file.

questions.prompt: A draft submission gives three pages of history before the decision needed appears on page four. What should the author change?

options.text: Keep the history first so that the minister reads the full story before the ask
Move the history into an annex and leave the decision on page four
Cut the options section so the history carries the argument
Open with the decision needed and the deadline, then give a short background

questions.hint: The ask and the deadline come first because the minister has limited time.

questions.prompt: Why does a submission normally include a recommendation, not only a list of options?

options.text: Ministers expect officials' professional judgement, which they are free to accept or reject
The minister is obliged to follow whichever option the officials recommend, so a recommendation settles the matter
A recommendation shows the department has already made the decision and only needs the minister's signature
Listing options without stating a view would breach political impartiality and expose the author to criticism

questions.hint: Officials advise and ministers decide, so a view is part of good advice.

questions.prompt: Which statement about private secretaries in a minister's office is correct?

options.text: They are party appointees who may help the minister with party work as well as official business
They are the minister's personal staff and so sit outside the Civil Service Code and its rules
They are civil servants bound by the Civil Service Code who manage the minister's papers
They are special advisers who are appointed by the minister and who leave when the minister does

questions.hint: Private office staff are permanent civil servants, unlike special advisers.

questions.prompt: The evidence shows the minister's favoured option performs worst on cost. What should the submission do?

options.text: Put the favoured option first and leave the cost comparison to the finance annex where it is less prominent
Set out the evidence fairly, state which option it supports and explain the favoured option's risks
Recommend the favoured option, since policy choices belong to the minister and officials should support them
Describe all the options neutrally and make no recommendation, so that nobody can say officials took a side

questions.hint: Honest advice sets out the evidence even when it is unwelcome.

questions.prompt: Finance has not yet cleared the cost figures and the deadline is tight. What is the best course?

options.text: Send it as cleared, since finance will almost certainly agree the figures when they get round to checking them
Say in the submission and to the private office that finance clearance is outstanding
Hold it back until finance clears it, however long that takes, even if the minister's deadline is missed
Take the cost section out so that the gap is not visible to the minister and the submission can go on time

questions.hint: Be open about what has not been cleared rather than implying it has.

questions.prompt: The minister's note on a submission says 'agree option B', but a phone call from the private office says the minister now wants option C. What should the official do?

options.text: Ask the private office to confirm the change in writing and record it on the file
Act on the phone call, because it is the most recent instruction from the minister's own office
Act on the written note, because a decision only counts when it is on paper and signed
Ask the special adviser which option the minister really meant and act on what they say

questions.hint: A changed instruction needs a written record so the decision trail is accurate.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in the handling section of a submission?

options.text: The author's view of how the decision might affect the governing party's poll ratings in the coming months
A list of everyone who commented on earlier drafts, with what each person said about the options
The planned announcement date, the lines for Parliament and the media, and who needs advance notice
A history of how earlier governments handled the policy, set out decade by decade for context

questions.hint: Handling covers how a decision will be communicated, not party politics.

questions.prompt: A clearing official passes a submission with an incorrect figure and it reaches the minister. Who is responsible for the error?

options.text: Only the private secretary, who handled the paper last and passed it to the minister
The minister, who signed the decision on the strength of the paper and so owns what it says
The Permanent Secretary alone, as head of the department and the person accountable for all its advice
The author and the clearing officials, which is why facts are checked before sign-off

questions.hint: Accuracy is owed by those who write and clear the advice.

items.title: L11: Answering parliamentary questions
items.source: House of Commons Procedure; Ministerial Code (accuracy and openness); Cabinet Office guidance for officials on parliamentary questions
items.body: MPs and peers put questions to ministers, either orally in the chamber or in writing. Written questions are answered by the minister in a reply published in Hansard, the official record. Officials in the department draft the reply, but it goes out as the minister's answer, and the minister is accountable to Parliament for it. The Ministerial Code requires ministers to give accurate and truthful information to Parliament and to correct any inadvertent error at the earliest opportunity. Information should be withheld only if disclosure would not be in the public interest, judged against the relevant rules, such as the Freedom of Information Act exemptions. A good draft answers the question that was asked, uses facts that can be checked, and is consistent with earlier answers on the same subject. Officials check figures with the data owner, clear the draft with policy colleagues, and often with press office and a legal adviser if the issue is sensitive. A named day question asks for an answer on a particular day, and departments are expected to meet that date or explain the delay. A holding reply may be sent where a full answer needs more time, but it should not be used to avoid answering. Where an answer is later found to be wrong, officials tell the private office quickly so the minister can correct the record.

questions.prompt: A written question asks how many cases were closed last year. The data team can supply only a figure for closed and reopened cases combined. What should the draft answer do?

options.text: Give the combined figure as though it answered the question, since it is the nearest number available
Give the figure with a clear note of what it covers, or say the exact figure is not held
Answer a related question for which the department has better numbers and leave the original unaddressed
Decline to answer because the exact figure requested is not held in the form the MP asked for

questions.hint: An answer must be accurate about what the data actually shows.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable to Parliament for a written answer drafted by an official?

options.text: The official who drafted it, as the author of the words
The Permanent Secretary, who clears every answer
The minister, who gives the answer in their own name
The Speaker, who approves answers before publication

questions.hint: Officials draft but ministers answer to Parliament.

questions.prompt: An official realises that a figure in a published answer was wrong. What should happen first?

options.text: Tell the private office promptly so the minister can correct the record at the earliest opportunity
Wait for the next routine answer on the topic and quietly use the correct figure in that one
Leave it unless an MP complains, since the error was not deliberate and nobody is likely to notice
Ask Hansard to amend the published answer so the official record shows the correct figure

questions.hint: The Code expects prompt correction of inadvertent errors.

questions.prompt: What is the proper use of a holding reply?

options.text: To close the question when the department has nothing it wishes to say on the subject
To postpone an answer that would be politically awkward until the issue has gone quiet
To replace the need for a named day answer once the date has been missed
To tell the MP that more time is needed, with a full answer to follow

questions.hint: Holding replies buy time; they are not a way to avoid answering.

questions.prompt: Which clearance is most likely before an answer on a sensitive topic goes to the minister?

options.text: The Treasury, whatever the topic, because every answer has some spending implication to check
Policy colleagues and the data owner, and often legal advisers and press office
The Cabinet Secretary in every case, since answers to Parliament are a matter of propriety
The opposition spokesperson, as a courtesy, so that nothing in the answer comes as a surprise

questions.hint: Clearance checks accuracy and handling before the minister sees it.

questions.prompt: A draft answer is accurate but says the opposite of an answer given three months ago, without explanation. What is the best action?

options.text: Send it as drafted, since the most recent answer is the one that counts for the record
Rewrite it to match the earlier answer, without checking whether the facts have changed
Flag the inconsistency to the private office and explain what changed
Ask for the earlier answer to be withdrawn from Hansard so that only one version remains

questions.hint: Consistency matters, and where things have changed the reason should be clear.

questions.prompt: When may a department decline to give information in an answer?

options.text: Where disclosure would not be in the public interest, judged against rules such as the FOI exemptions
Whenever the minister would prefer not to provide it, since ministers decide what Parliament is told
Whenever the information would be embarrassing for the department or reveal a mistake by officials
Only if the Speaker has agreed to the refusal in advance, which is always required for a refusal

questions.hint: Withholding needs a proper basis, not mere preference.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Hansard in this process?

options.text: It is a private log kept by each department of the advice it has given to ministers
It is the list of questions that ministers have refused to answer in the current session
It is the monthly summary of each department's performance against its published targets
It is the official record of what was said and answered in Parliament

questions.hint: Answers published in Hansard form a public record.

items.title: L11: Letters from MPs and ministerial correspondence
items.source: Cabinet Office guidance on handling ministerial correspondence; ICO guidance on disclosing personal data to elected representatives
items.body: Departments receive large volumes of letters and emails addressed to ministers, many from MPs writing on behalf of constituents. Most are handled by a ministerial correspondence unit, which logs each item, finds the right policy or operational team to draft a reply, and tracks it against a target. Departments set their own targets for answering, often around fifteen working days, and publish performance information. A reply is drafted for the minister's signature, or for an official to sign on the minister's behalf when the issue is operational. Replies should answer the points raised, explain the department's position clearly and in plain English, avoid jargon, and say what the person can do next, for example how to appeal or complain. An MP writing for a constituent is normally acting on that person's behalf, so the department can usually reply with that person's information, but it should check that the person really is the MP's constituent and share only what is needed for the case. It should never disclose details about other people. Replies must be accurate and consistent with published policy; officials should not make promises the department cannot keep or commit the minister to something they have not agreed. Ministerial letters are official records and may be disclosed under the Freedom of Information Act, so they should be written with that in mind.

questions.prompt: An MP writes for a constituent about a delayed payment. The case file also holds information about the constituent's partner. What should the reply contain?

options.text: Everything on the file, because an MP is entitled to see all of the information the department holds
A summary of the whole household's circumstances, so that the MP has the complete picture of the case
Information about the constituent's own case, leaving out the partner's details unless they agree
Only a general statement about the policy, since MPs cannot lawfully receive anyone's personal data

questions.hint: Share what is needed for the constituent's case and not other people's data.

questions.prompt: A letter from an MP does not say whether the person concerned lives in the MP's constituency. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Reply in full, on the assumption that an MP who writes about a person is always acting properly
Send the reply directly to the person named, copying in the MP so that both of them are informed
Return the letter, saying that it falls outside the ministerial correspondence process altogether
Check that the MP is acting for one of their constituents before sharing personal details

questions.hint: Confirming the MP is acting for the person protects personal data.

questions.prompt: Who normally signs a reply about a routine operational decision, such as a delayed claim?

options.text: An official, on behalf of the minister
The Permanent Secretary personally
The Prime Minister's office
The special adviser, who speaks for the minister

questions.hint: Operational answers are often signed by officials on the minister's behalf.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes a ministerial reply better?

options.text: It lists every policy document on the topic, to show that the department has been thorough
It answers the points raised, uses plain English and says what the person can do next
It promises a quick resolution, so that the person feels reassured about what will happen next
It avoids stating the department's position on the case, so that the department keeps its options open

questions.hint: A good reply is clear, accurate and gives next steps.

questions.prompt: A draft reply promises the constituent a payment 'within days', but only the delivery team can decide this. What is the main problem?

options.text: It is too short to count as a proper reply to an MP writing on behalf of a constituent
It should have been addressed to the delivery team and not to the MP who wrote the letter
It commits the department to something that has not been agreed or checked
Promises of any kind are forbidden in ministerial letters, so any commitment is a breach of the rules

questions.hint: Officials must not make commitments the department has not agreed.

questions.prompt: Why should a ministerial letter be written with the Freedom of Information Act in mind?

options.text: Letters to MPs are published automatically once they are signed, so they should be written for the public
The Act covers only letters about public spending, so it affects only finance correspondence
The Act forbids any personal data in a reply, so replies must be general in tone
Official correspondence is a record that may later be requested and disclosed

questions.hint: Correspondence is an official record that may be disclosed.

questions.prompt: What does a ministerial correspondence unit typically do?

options.text: Log letters, send them to the right team to draft, and track replies against the target
Decide the department's policy on each issue that is raised in the letters it receives
Write every reply itself without the policy team's input, to keep the department's tone consistent
Forward all MP letters to the Cabinet Office, which then prepares the reply on the department's behalf

questions.hint: The unit manages the process; policy teams provide the content.

questions.prompt: The target reply time is nearly up and the full answer is not ready. What is the best approach?

options.text: Send a brief reply that sidesteps the questions asked, so that the target is technically met
Send a short interim reply explaining the delay and when to expect the full answer
Let the target pass, since accuracy matters more than timing and an interim reply looks weak
Ask the MP to send the letter again once the answer is ready, so that the clock restarts

questions.hint: An interim reply is honest about the delay without giving a poor answer.

items.title: L11: Giving evidence to a select committee
items.source: Cabinet Office, Departmental Evidence and Response to Select Committees (the Osmotherly Rules); House of Commons liaison and select committee guidance
items.body: Select committees are cross-party groups of MPs, or in the Lords of peers, that examine the work of government departments and other topics. They can take written and oral evidence and publish reports to which the government normally responds in writing, usually within two months. Officials who appear before a committee do so on behalf of their minister. Government guidance, often called the Osmotherly Rules after the official who first compiled it, sets out how departments should co-operate. The general principle is to be as open and helpful as possible. Ministers, not committees, decide which official represents the department, although a committee may name the person it wants, and the minister normally accepts. Officials are expected to explain policy, facts and how decisions were made; they do not usually discuss the advice they gave to ministers, because that is confidential, nor do they comment on the merits of policy, which is for ministers. Senior officials who are accounting officers do answer for how money is managed. Evidence must be accurate and should not mislead; if an official realises something said was wrong, they should write to the committee as soon as possible to correct it. Officials usually receive briefing in advance, rehearse possible questions and agree with the private office what information can be provided.

questions.prompt: A committee member asks an official exactly what advice they gave the minister on a decision. What is the usual response?

options.text: Explain the facts and the process, but say that advice to ministers is confidential
Read out the advice in full, since the committee has asked for it and has a right to hear it
Say that only the minister may discuss it, and decline to say anything else on the subject
Decline to answer anything further in the session until the minister has been consulted about it

questions.hint: Advice to ministers is generally confidential, but the process can be explained.

questions.prompt: During evidence an official realises a figure they gave was wrong. What should they do?

options.text: Wait to see whether the committee notices the mistake
Correct it only if a journalist raises the matter
Write to the committee as soon as possible to correct it
Raise it at the minister's next appearance instead

questions.hint: Prompt correction keeps the committee properly informed.

questions.prompt: Who decides which official represents the department before a committee?

options.text: The committee clerk, who chooses which officials attend whatever the department may prefer
The Cabinet Office, which assigns officials to committees according to their grade and expertise
The Speaker of the House of Commons, who rules on which witnesses are called to attend
The minister, though a committee's request for a named person is normally accepted

questions.hint: Ministers choose, with a committee's named request usually respected.

questions.prompt: An official is asked whether a policy is the right one. What is the best response?

options.text: Give a personal view on whether the policy is wise, since the committee is asking for an expert opinion
Explain what the policy aims to do and how it works, leaving its merits to ministers
Say the question is unfair and decline to discuss the policy at all during the session
Describe how an alternative policy proposed by the opposition would differ from the current one

questions.hint: Policy merits are for ministers; officials explain and describe.

questions.prompt: Why do officials rehearse before an evidence session?

options.text: To prepare accurate answers, agree what can be shared and anticipate questions
To agree answers that avoid telling the committee anything of substance
Because the committee sends its exact questions in advance
Because the Osmotherly Rules require a formal practice session

questions.hint: Preparation supports accurate and helpful evidence, not evasion.

questions.prompt: Who within a department will usually be asked about how public money was managed?

options.text: The special adviser, who tracks spending for the minister and is closest to the budget decisions
The private secretary, who controls the minister's budget and signs off the department's spending
The accounting officer, normally the Permanent Secretary or a delegated chief executive
The press officer, who explains the department's financial decisions to the media and to MPs

questions.hint: Accounting officers answer for the management of public money.

questions.prompt: What does the government normally do after a select committee report?

options.text: Ignore the report unless the House of Commons votes on it, since it is only advisory
Respond in writing within a set period, usually two months
Publish a reply drafted by the committee, which the department then agrees without changes
Ask the Speaker to summarise the report for ministers before any response is prepared

questions.hint: The government usually replies in writing to committee reports.

questions.prompt: Which approach best reflects the guidance on co-operation?

options.text: Provide only what is directly asked and nothing more, to protect the department and its ministers
Treat every request as a risk to the minister and delay the reply for as long as the rules allow
Give the committee full internal advice whenever it asks, as the committee is entitled to see everything
Be as open and helpful as possible, withholding only for good reason and saying so

questions.hint: The principle is openness, with confidentiality for advice to ministers.

items.title: L11: The National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee
items.source: National Audit Office, About us; Parliament.uk, Public Accounts Committee; HM Treasury, Managing Public Money
items.body: The Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) is an officer of the House of Commons who leads the National Audit Office (NAO). The NAO is independent of government. It audits the accounts of government departments and many other public bodies, and it carries out value for money studies that examine whether public spending has achieved its objectives economically, efficiently and effectively. It does not question the merits of the government's policy objectives; it examines how they were delivered. The NAO's reports go to Parliament, where the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), a cross-party committee normally chaired by a member of the opposition, takes evidence on them. Accounting officers, usually Permanent Secretaries or chief executives of arm's length bodies, are called to explain what happened and what will change. The PAC publishes a report with recommendations and the Treasury responds to them in a document called a Treasury Minute, in which government sets out how it will act. Officials supporting such a session help prepare factual briefing, check figures, agree what lessons have been learned and keep a clear record of action taken after the hearing. A department that gives an incomplete picture to the NAO or PAC risks damaging trust and the accounting officer's reputation. The audit certificate on departmental accounts states whether they give a true and fair view and whether spending was regular.

questions.prompt: An NAO report criticises how a department delivered a programme. Which question is the NAO most likely to be examining?

options.text: Whether the minister's policy aim was a wise choice for the country
Whether the opposition would have run the programme differently
Whether the programme delivered value for money against its objectives
Whether ministers gave clear instructions to officials

questions.hint: The NAO looks at delivery and value for money, not the merits of policy objectives.

questions.prompt: Who normally chairs the Public Accounts Committee?

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor General
A member of the main opposition party
The Chancellor of the Exchequer
A government minister chosen by the Prime Minister

questions.hint: By convention the PAC chair is an opposition MP.

questions.prompt: What is a Treasury Minute?

options.text: The record of a meeting between Treasury ministers and the heads of the main departments
A note of the minimum spend that the Treasury allows in any department before approval is needed
A statement from the NAO about an audit that is under way and the findings so far
The government's response to PAC recommendations, setting out how it will act

questions.hint: Treasury Minutes record the government's response to PAC reports.

questions.prompt: An official preparing an accounting officer for a PAC hearing finds that a key fact in the department's evidence to the NAO was inaccurate. What is the right step?

options.text: Raise it immediately so it can be corrected with the NAO and the committee
Leave it out of the briefing so that the accounting officer is not worried by it before the hearing
Wait to see whether the committee asks a question that touches on it before saying anything
Correct it in the department's internal records only, since the NAO has already published its report

questions.hint: An error in evidence to the NAO needs prompt correction.

questions.prompt: Why is the NAO's independence from government important?

options.text: It lets the NAO change government policy directly where it finds that spending has failed
It allows the NAO to audit only the bodies it chooses and to ignore the rest of government
It means ministers cannot read a report before publication, whatever the factual accuracy of its contents
It can report to Parliament on spending without direction from ministers

questions.hint: Independence lets the NAO give Parliament an impartial account.

questions.prompt: Who usually appears before the PAC for a department?

options.text: The accounting officer, normally the Permanent Secretary
The minister responsible for the policy, answering for the decisions that were taken
The department's special advisers, who explain the political reasons for the spending
The Comptroller and Auditor General, defending the findings in the report to the committee

questions.hint: PAC hearings are with accounting officers.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the audit certificate on departmental accounts is correct?

options.text: It states whether the policy that was funded has public support and delivers its aims
It says whether accounts give a true and fair view and whether spending was regular
It confirms that the decisions taken by the minister were correct and well judged
It is issued by the Treasury, which signs off every department's accounts before publication

questions.hint: The C&AG certifies accounts and the regularity of spending.

questions.prompt: After a hearing, what should an official supporting the department do?

options.text: Archive the papers and take no further action until the report comes out
Brief the media on the result before the report is published
Track the actions promised and keep a clear record of what has been done
Ask the NAO to withdraw recommendations the department disagrees with

questions.hint: Following up commitments shows lessons are acted on.

items.title: L11: Framework documents and sponsoring an arm's-length body
items.source: Cabinet Office and HM Treasury, Public Bodies Handbook and arm's-length body guidance; Managing Public Money
items.body: A government department that creates or oversees an arm's-length body (ALB) is known as its sponsor department. The relationship is set out in a framework document, which records the body's purpose, status, governance, financial delegations, reporting lines and how the department will review it. A sponsor team in the department is the day-to-day link: it advises ministers on the body, gives assurance that public money is spent properly, challenges performance, and helps the body understand government priorities. The body usually has a chair and board. The chair is often appointed by a minister through a regulated public appointments process, and the chief executive is normally the body's accounting officer, designated by the department's Permanent Secretary. The body is accountable to Parliament through the sponsoring minister, but day-to-day decisions are taken by the body, not the minister. A good sponsor team does not run the body. It keeps regular contact, reviews risk, agrees budgets, and makes sure the chair and minister have a good working relationship. Where the body is not meeting objectives or there is a concern about governance, the sponsor team escalates to the Director or Permanent Secretary. Departments also review each body from time to time, to check that it is still needed, that its functions are performed well, and that its governance is working. Framework documents should be reviewed regularly and updated when the body's role changes.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a framework document?

options.text: To list the policy decisions that ministers have made for the body and that it must now carry out
To record the pay, grades and conditions of all the staff employed by the body
To give the body's board formal power to change its own status without further approval
To set out the body's purpose, governance, financial delegations and its relationship with the sponsor

questions.hint: A framework document records how the body and department will work together.

questions.prompt: A sponsor team notices that an ALB's finance director has left and no replacement is in place. What would be the proper response?

options.text: Raise it with the body, ask how it will manage the risk and escalate if the gap persists
Appoint a departmental official to run the body's finances at once, to protect public money
Wait until the annual report to see whether the body mentions the gap in its own account
Tell the minister that the body is failing and recommend that it should be closed down

questions.hint: Sponsors challenge and escalate without taking over the body's functions.

questions.prompt: Which role is usually the accounting officer of an ALB?

options.text: The chair of the board, appointed by the minister and responsible for how the body is run
The sponsor team's head of branch, who oversees the body's budget on behalf of the department
The chief executive, designated by the department's Permanent Secretary
The Treasury's director of public spending, who holds the accounts of every public body

questions.hint: The chief executive is normally designated as accounting officer.

questions.prompt: Who answers to Parliament for the body's operation?

options.text: The chair of the body, who appears before a select committee to answer for it in all cases
The sponsoring minister, although the body takes day-to-day decisions
The Treasury, as the funder of every public body and the department that sets the rules
The Civil Service Commission, which oversees the conduct of all bodies receiving public money

questions.hint: Ministers answer to Parliament for sponsored bodies.

questions.prompt: How should a sponsor team approach the body's operational decisions?

options.text: Respect the body's independence in them, while checking governance and results
Approve each operational decision before it is made, so that the department stays in control
Take over decisions that the minister has concerns about, until the matter has been resolved
Keep out of the body's business altogether until a crisis arises and the minister asks for action

questions.hint: The sponsor oversees; it does not run the body.

questions.prompt: Why does the department review each ALB from time to time?

options.text: To decide which of the body's staff should be brought back into the department as civil servants
To check the body is still needed, performing well and properly governed
To make sure the body's chair shares the minister's political views and will follow the minister's line
Because the framework document expires automatically each year and has to be replaced

questions.hint: Periodic reviews test whether the body still works and is still needed.

questions.prompt: New legislation gives an ALB extra duties. What should happen to its framework document?

options.text: It should stay as it is, since it records the original purpose
It should be replaced by a letter from the minister
It should be reviewed and updated to reflect the new role
It should be withdrawn until the next body review

questions.hint: Framework documents should keep pace with a body's role.

questions.prompt: Who normally appoints the chair of a body such as this?

options.text: The body's own board, by an internal election when the previous chair's term ends
The Permanent Secretary alone, after discussion with the sponsor team and the body's chief executive
The Civil Service Commission, which makes every public appointment on the minister's behalf
A minister, through a regulated public appointments process

questions.hint: Chairs are commonly appointed by ministers under a regulated process.

items.title: L11: Devolved governments: what officials should know in practice
items.source: GOV.UK, Devolution settlement guidance; Government of Wales Act 2006; Scotland Act 1998; Northern Ireland Act 1998; Sewel convention
items.body: The UK has three devolved governments: the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government and the Northern Ireland Executive, each answerable to its own legislature. Scottish Government and Welsh Government staff belong to the UK Home Civil Service, while Northern Ireland has its own separate Northern Ireland Civil Service. In Scotland and Wales, powers are devolved by listing reserved matters, which stay with the UK Parliament, and anything not reserved is devolved. Northern Ireland has excepted and reserved matters, with the rest transferred. Many areas, such as health, education, housing and much of transport, are devolved, while defence and foreign affairs stay at UK level. UK government officials and devolved officials work as officials of different governments: they co-operate, share information and plan jointly, but neither administration directs the other. The Sewel convention says the UK Parliament will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature, which it usually gives through a legislative consent motion. Where a UK Bill touches devolved matters, officials should talk to their devolved counterparts early. Financial arrangements matter too: the devolved governments receive a block grant, adjusted by the Barnett formula, and have some tax powers. A UK policy can have different effects across the nations, so officials should check whether a policy covers the whole UK or only England.

questions.prompt: A policy paper says it will 'apply across the UK', but it covers health services. What should an official check first?

options.text: Whether the Prime Minister has approved the policy for the whole UK, which would settle the matter
Whether health is devolved, so that the policy applies only in England unless devolved governments agree
Whether the department can direct devolved health services, since the paper says UK-wide delivery
Whether the Barnett formula has been applied to the policy, because that decides where it applies

questions.hint: Devolved matters need agreement with the relevant government, not assumption.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the civil servants of the devolved governments is correct?

options.text: Scottish and Welsh Government staff are in the Home Civil Service; Northern Ireland has its own
All three devolved governments share a separate Civil Service that is distinct from the Home Civil Service
None of the devolved governments employ civil servants, since their staff are local government employees
Only Northern Ireland staff belong to the Home Civil Service, while Scotland and Wales have their own

questions.hint: Northern Ireland has a separate Civil Service; Scotland and Wales do not.

questions.prompt: What does the Sewel convention say?

options.text: The UK Parliament may never legislate on devolved matters under any circumstances at all
Devolved governments must follow the lead of UK ministers on every area of policy that overlaps
The UK Parliament will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the devolved legislature's consent
Devolved legislatures hold a veto over every UK Bill, whether or not it touches a devolved matter

questions.hint: It is a convention, not a veto, but it is normally observed.

questions.prompt: A UK Bill touches an area devolved to Wales. When should officials contact their Welsh counterparts?

options.text: After the Bill is introduced to Parliament, once the text is settled and there is something to share
Only if the Welsh Government asks about it, since the devolved government must first raise concerns
After Royal Assent, once the final text is fixed and the legislation has been agreed by Parliament
Early in the policy design, so consent can be sought and concerns raised

questions.hint: Early engagement is better practice than late notice.

questions.prompt: How is the funding of the devolved governments mainly provided?

options.text: Direct payments from the Treasury to each devolved department, agreed one department at a time
Fees charged to each devolved government for every service that the UK Government provides to it
Grants requested one by one from the Cabinet Office, which assesses each bid separately
A block grant adjusted by the Barnett formula, plus some devolved taxes

questions.hint: The block grant and Barnett adjustment are the core mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Defence is devolved to the three governments, while education is reserved to the UK Parliament
Defence is generally reserved to the UK; education is generally devolved
Both defence and education are devolved, with the UK Government keeping only the right to advise
Both are reserved to the UK in every case, with devolved governments delivering on the UK's behalf

questions.hint: Defence stays at UK level; education is generally devolved.

questions.prompt: How do UK officials and devolved officials generally relate to one another?

options.text: As officials of different governments who co-operate but do not direct each other
As line managers and staff in a single department, with the UK side giving the instructions
As rivals who must compete with each other for resources and for ministers' attention
As members of one government with a single policy position, agreed by the Cabinet Office

questions.hint: Devolved governments are separate governments, not parts of UK departments.

questions.prompt: A UK minister announces a scheme that applies to England only, but a press note says 'the UK'. What is the correct response?

options.text: Leave the wording as it is, since most readers will be in England and will understand the point
Ask the devolved governments to copy the scheme, so that the wording becomes accurate
Correct the wording so it makes clear that the scheme applies to England
Add a line saying the scheme is devolved and so does not need to apply to the rest of the UK

questions.hint: Accuracy about territorial extent avoids misleading the public.

items.title: L11: Special advisers and what they may and may not do
items.source: Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010; Code of Conduct for Special Advisers; Civil Service Code
items.body: Special advisers are temporary civil servants appointed by a minister, with the Prime Minister's approval, to give political advice. They are an exception to the rule that civil servants are appointed on merit, and their appointments end when the minister leaves office. The Code of Conduct for Special Advisers says they must not do anything that conflicts with the Civil Service Code, apart from the requirements of impartiality and objectivity. They may advise ministers on the political aspects of policy, represent the minister's views, and liaise with the party. They may ask for information and may see official papers, subject to the minister's agreement. They may not manage civil servants or give them orders, apart from a few senior special advisers in Number 10 who are authorised by an Order in Council. They cannot authorise spending of public money, and they cannot ask civil servants to do party political work. If a special adviser asks you to do something you think is inappropriate, you should discuss it with your line manager or ask the private office, and use the Code's normal routes if it is not resolved. Officials should treat special advisers with courtesy, be open about any problems, and not be afraid to say that a request is outside what they can do.

questions.prompt: A special adviser asks an official to draft a press release attacking the opposition's policy using the department's resources. What is the right response?

options.text: Draft it, because special advisers speak for the minister and have the authority to ask for it
Draft it in the evening, so that no official time is used and nobody can complain
Decline, explaining that party political material is outside official duties, and tell the line manager
Draft it, but send it to the opposition for comment first so that it is fair

questions.hint: Civil servants cannot be asked to produce party political material.

questions.prompt: A special adviser tells a civil servant to change a figure in a briefing to show a better result. What should the official do?

options.text: Refuse to alter the facts and raise it with their line manager
Alter it, since the adviser represents the minister and has the authority to decide the line
Alter it but add a footnote with the original figure, so the true position is still visible
Ask for the instruction in writing and then comply, since a written request covers the official

questions.hint: Honesty and objectivity cannot be set aside by a request.

questions.prompt: Which statement about special advisers is correct?

options.text: They are permanent civil servants appointed after open competition and stay when ministers change
They are party officials with no official status, employed and paid by the political party
They are appointed by the Civil Service Commission after a merit-based recruitment campaign
They are temporary civil servants appointed by a minister, whose appointment ends when the minister leaves

questions.hint: Special advisers are temporary and appointed by ministers, with the Prime Minister's approval.

questions.prompt: What is the position on a special adviser authorising spending of public money?

options.text: A special adviser may approve spending within the minister's budget, since they work for the minister
Advisers cannot authorise expenditure or manage civil servants other than other special advisers
A special adviser may approve spending once the Permanent Secretary agrees to the request
A special adviser may approve spending only from the private office budget, up to a set limit

questions.hint: Special advisers cannot authorise expenditure.

questions.prompt: A special adviser asks to see the draft submission before it goes to the minister. What is the usual position?

options.text: Never, because advisers are not permitted to see official papers prepared by civil servants
Only after the minister has made a decision, so that advisers cannot influence the advice
The adviser may see it with the minister's agreement, because they advise on its political aspects
Only with the written approval of the Cabinet Secretary, who controls access to such papers

questions.hint: Special advisers may see papers, subject to the minister's agreement.

questions.prompt: Why are special advisers an exception to the rule of recruitment on merit?

options.text: They hold roles that are not considered part of government, so the rule does not apply to them
They give a minister political advice, so are temporary and personal to that minister
They were appointed before the Civil Service Commission existed, so the rule was never applied
They are treated as volunteers rather than employees, so recruitment rules do not cover them

questions.hint: They are appointed under a special statutory route for political advice.

questions.prompt: A special adviser is rude and demanding towards an AO. What should the AO do?

options.text: Accept it, since advisers carry the minister's authority and are entitled to expect compliance
Ignore any instructions from that adviser in future, so that the problem does not recur
Complain directly to the press, so that the matter is dealt with in public
Raise it with their line manager, who can take it up through the private office

questions.hint: Poor treatment is a conduct matter for line management.

questions.prompt: Which activity is a special adviser allowed to carry out?

options.text: Advising a minister on the political presentation of a policy
Giving orders to the department's senior civil servants on behalf of the minister
Using official resources to campaign for the party at a by-election
Signing off the department's accounts as the minister's delegate

questions.hint: Political advice to the minister is the core permitted role.

items.title: L11: Keeping a decision record
items.source: Public Records Act 1958; National Archives, Information and Records Management guidance; Cabinet Office guidance on official records and instant messaging
items.body: Good government depends on a reliable record of what was decided, by whom, on what advice and why. Under the Public Records Act 1958, departments have a duty to keep records of value and to transfer selected records to The National Archives, normally after a period of years. A decision record should show who made the decision and their authority, what options and evidence were considered, the advice received, any risks or dissent, the reasons, and the date. It should be stored in the department's proper records system, not only in a personal inbox, notebook or private device, so that others can find it and so that it is available if a decision is later reviewed or challenged. Information held by the department may be requested under the Freedom of Information Act or data protection law, so notes should be professional, factual and fair. Guidance says that instant messaging and similar tools may be used for convenience, but if they are used to take or record decisions, the content must be moved into the official record. Officials who are not sure whether a record is worth keeping should usually keep it. A meeting note should name who attended, set out decisions and actions, and say who is responsible for each. Failing to keep an adequate record can weaken a department's position in a judicial review, an inquiry or an audit.

questions.prompt: A decision was agreed in a quick messaging chat between three officials. What should happen next?

options.text: Record the decision and the reasons in the official records system
Delete the chat to avoid confusion over which version of the decision is correct
Leave it in the chat, as the three officials will remember what was agreed
Forward the chat to a personal email account so that it is kept safely

questions.hint: Decisions taken informally still need to be captured in the official record.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of what a decision record should show?

options.text: Only the final choice made, to keep the record short and easy to read later
The names of any officials who disagreed with the decision and the reasons they gave
Only the advice that the minister accepted, since the rest is no longer relevant
Who decided, on what authority, which options and advice were considered, and why

questions.hint: The record should let a later reader understand the decision.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to keep decision records only in a personal notebook?

options.text: Notebooks are forbidden by law, so any decision recorded in one is invalid and must be taken again
A notebook is never accepted as evidence in an inquiry, whatever it records and whoever kept it
Others cannot find them, and they may not be available if the decision is reviewed or requested under FOI
Notes in a notebook must be destroyed after a week under the department's retention rules

questions.hint: Corporate records must be accessible to the organisation.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Records Act 1958 require of departments?

options.text: To publish every record on GOV.UK within a year of its creation, so the public can see it
To keep records of value and transfer selected ones to The National Archives
To destroy all records after one year unless a minister asks for them to be kept
To give the Civil Service Commission a copy of every file that the department creates

questions.hint: It governs preserving and transferring public records.

questions.prompt: An official is unsure whether a short email exchange is worth keeping. What is the usual advice?

options.text: Delete it, to avoid clutter in the system and keep the records easy to search
Keep it, or ask the records team, rather than deleting it
Keep it only if a minister was copied into the exchange, since only those matter
Print it and keep it in a personal file, which is the safest way to preserve it

questions.hint: Where unsure, keep the record.

questions.prompt: A meeting note records only 'It was agreed to proceed'. What is missing?

options.text: Who attended, the detail of the decision, the actions and who is responsible for each
A signature from the Permanent Secretary, which every meeting note needs before it can be filed
The personal opinions of each attendee, so that it is clear how each person voted on the matter
A list of the other meetings held that week, so the reader can see the context of the decision

questions.hint: Notes should set out decisions, actions and owners.

questions.prompt: How might a poor record of a decision affect the department later?

options.text: It can remove the need for any further review, since there is nothing to examine
It automatically cancels the decision, because an unrecorded decision has no legal effect
It prevents anyone from asking about the matter under the Freedom of Information Act
It can weaken the department's position in a judicial review, inquiry or audit

questions.hint: Missing records make decisions difficult to defend.

questions.prompt: Why should meeting notes be factual, professional and fair?

options.text: Only managers are allowed to write notes, so tone is a matter for the manager
Notes are published automatically after a meeting, so they have to be polite
They may be disclosed under the Freedom of Information Act or data protection law
Notes are used to appraise the author's performance, so they must be written carefully

questions.hint: Records can be requested later, so tone and accuracy matter.

items.title: L11: Delegated authority and who can sign
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money; Government Functional Standards (Finance); departmental delegation letters
items.body: Departments run on delegation. The Permanent Secretary, as accounting officer, holds overall responsibility for the department's spending, and delegates authority in writing to budget holders and others, usually in a delegation letter. Each delegation sets out what the person may approve, up to what financial limit, and for what purpose. Staff should only sign or approve within the authority given to them. Anything outside the limit, or of a new, novel, contentious or repercussive kind, must be referred up, and in some cases to the Treasury for approval. A basic safeguard is separation of duties: the person who requests spending should not be the one who approves it, and the person who approves it should not also be the one who pays it. Another is that approvals should be in writing and kept with the file. Staff may not split a single purchase into smaller ones in order to bring each below a limit, because that would defeat the control. When a manager is absent, the delegation does not automatically pass to a deputy; the deputy needs their own delegation or a formal cover arrangement. Staff who exceed their delegated authority may cause irregular spending, which the accounting officer has to report and may have to explain to Parliament. Anyone who is unsure should ask their finance business partner before they commit the department.

questions.prompt: An EO has authority to approve spending up to a set limit. A purchase would cost slightly more than that limit. What is the correct step?

options.text: Approve it, as the difference is small and the finance team can regularise it later
Split it into two purchases that each fall under the limit, so that both can be approved
Approve it and tell the manager afterwards, since it is within the spirit of the delegation
Refer it to someone with the appropriate delegation before committing

questions.hint: Authority is capped at the limit, however small the excess.

questions.prompt: Why should the person requesting spend not also approve it?

options.text: Requesters do not usually understand the budget
The Treasury requires every request to be anonymous
Separation of duties helps prevent error and fraud
Approval must always come from outside the department

questions.hint: Separation of duties is a standard control.

questions.prompt: A manager is on leave and nobody has been given a formal cover delegation. What should happen to urgent approvals?

options.text: Arrange a proper cover delegation or escalate to someone who holds the authority
Let the most senior team member approve them informally, until the manager returns from leave
Wait until the manager returns, whatever the cost to the work that is waiting for approval
Approve them in the manager's name, as the manager would have given the same approval

questions.hint: Delegation does not pass to a deputy by default.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with splitting a large purchase into several smaller ones?

options.text: It always increases the total cost
It avoids the approval limit and defeats the control
It is acceptable if the goods are ordered on different days
It breaches data protection rules

questions.hint: Splitting to get under a limit is a recognised abuse of the control.

questions.prompt: Who is the source of financial delegations in a department?

options.text: The accounting officer, who delegates in writing to budget holders
The Cabinet Office, which sets each person's limit and sends it out to departments
The National Audit Office, which proposes the limits after each audit of the department
Each team leader, who decides what their own team members may approve as they see fit

questions.hint: The accounting officer delegates through formal letters.

questions.prompt: Which type of proposal usually needs Treasury approval even if the department has a delegated limit?

options.text: One that is lower than the delegated limit but is of a type the department often uses
One that has been used in previous years and has already been through a review
One that is already in the budget, since the Treasury has to approve all budgeted spending
One that is novel, contentious or repercussive

questions.hint: Treasury control extends to these categories beyond normal limits.

questions.prompt: What may happen if an official spends beyond their delegated authority?

options.text: The Treasury will automatically accept it after the event, since the money has already been spent
The spending may be treated as irregular and the accounting officer may have to report it
It will be counted as value for money if the outcome was good and the department benefited
It will be recorded as a gift to the department, so no further action will be needed

questions.hint: Irregular spending can lead to reporting and explanation.

questions.prompt: Why should approvals be in writing?

options.text: Verbal approvals are always illegal under the rules on spending public money
The Treasury insists on paper copies of all approvals for its own audit purposes
So there is a clear record of who authorised what, and when
Handwritten notes are considered the most reliable form of evidence in an audit

questions.hint: Written approvals support accountability and audit.

items.title: L11: The centre of government: who does what
items.source: GOV.UK, Cabinet Office and HM Treasury about pages; Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010; Cabinet Manual
items.body: A small number of bodies at the centre co-ordinate the rest of government. Number 10 is the Prime Minister's office and residence, supporting the Prime Minister to set direction and manage the government's business. The Cabinet Office supports the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, co-ordinates policy across departments, runs the Cabinet's committees and the Civil Service's corporate functions, such as civil service human resources, and is responsible for propriety and ethics matters. The Cabinet Secretary leads the Cabinet Office, advises the Prime Minister, and is also Head of the Civil Service. HM Treasury is the government's economics and finance ministry. It sets the framework for public spending, runs the spending reviews, controls the rules in Managing Public Money, and advises on economic and tax policy. The Government Legal Department provides legal advice to departments. Other bodies, such as the Government Digital Service within the Cabinet Office, set cross-government standards. Each department keeps responsibility for its own policy and delivery, and central bodies act through guidance, standards, controls and co-ordination rather than taking over departmental work. Officials who face a question that crosses departments should usually talk to the relevant central team early, because it saves time and avoids mixed messages. In an emergency, the Cabinet Office co-ordinates the response through its civil contingencies arrangements.

questions.prompt: A department wants to know the rules for approving a new spending programme. Which central body is the primary source?

options.text: HM Treasury, through Managing Public Money and its spending controls
The Cabinet Office, which sets rules for every department
The National Audit Office, which approves programmes before they begin
Number 10, which signs off each spending line

questions.hint: The Treasury sets the framework for public spending.

questions.prompt: Who is the Head of the Civil Service?

options.text: The Prime Minister
The Chancellor of the Exchequer
The Cabinet Secretary
The Chair of the Civil Service Commission

questions.hint: The Cabinet Secretary leads the Cabinet Office and the Civil Service.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Cabinet Office is correct?

options.text: It sets economic policy and tax rates for the government and runs the spending reviews
It supports the Prime Minister and Cabinet and co-ordinates cross-government work
It audits the accounts of government departments on behalf of Parliament each year
It delivers most public services directly to the public through its network of offices

questions.hint: Co-ordination and corporate functions are central tasks.

questions.prompt: An official needs advice on the legality of a proposed power. Where should they usually go?

options.text: To the Cabinet Secretary, who is responsible for the legality of all government actions
To the Treasury, which decides whether any proposal is lawful before it can proceed
To a special adviser, who can arrange for a legal opinion on the minister's behalf
To the department's legal advisers, who come from the Government Legal Department

questions.hint: Government lawyers provide the legal advice.

questions.prompt: How do central bodies normally influence departments?

options.text: By taking over the delivery of departmental services where the centre believes it can do better
Through guidance, standards, controls and co-ordination, leaving departments responsible for their work
By appointing the department's staff directly, so that standards are the same in every department
By closing departments that perform poorly and moving their functions to the Cabinet Office

questions.hint: Departments keep responsibility for policy and delivery.

questions.prompt: Why talk to the relevant central team early on a cross-government issue?

options.text: Central teams must approve every proposal before it can be taken any further forward
The Civil Service Code requires officials to consult them before any cross-government work
It saves time and avoids mixed messages between departments
It is the only way to get the minister's agreement to the proposal in the first place

questions.hint: Early engagement helps co-ordination.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the responsibility of Number 10 rather than a department?

options.text: Running the passport service, which the Prime Minister's office oversees day to day
Collecting taxes on behalf of the Prime Minister, who is also First Lord of the Treasury
Auditing departments' accounts before they are laid before Parliament each year
Supporting the Prime Minister to set direction and manage the government's business

questions.hint: Number 10 is the Prime Minister's office.

questions.prompt: Who co-ordinates the central response in a national emergency?

options.text: The Cabinet Office, through its civil contingencies arrangements
The National Audit Office, which reviews emergency responses while they are under way
The Civil Service Commission, which directs civil servants during a national emergency
Each department independently, with no need for co-ordination from the centre of government

questions.hint: The Cabinet Office leads the centre's emergency co-ordination.

items.title: L11: Types of public body in real scenarios
items.source: Cabinet Office, Public Bodies guidance; GOV.UK, How government works
items.body: Government delivers through several kinds of organisation. Ministerial departments are led by a secretary of state. Non-ministerial departments, such as HM Revenue and Customs, have no minister directly in charge of day-to-day work but are still accountable to Parliament through a minister, and are often independent in regulatory or similar functions. Executive agencies, such as the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, are part of a department but have a chief executive and a degree of operational freedom set out in a framework document. Non-departmental public bodies (NDPBs) work at arm's length from ministers. They include executive NDPBs, which carry out public functions such as regulation or distribution of funds, advisory NDPBs, which give independent expert advice, and tribunal NDPBs, which hear appeals. Public corporations, such as the BBC, are largely independent and are accountable in other ways. Different forms exist because the government may want different things. A body that needs to be independent of ministers, such as a regulator or a tribunal, is more likely to be an NDPB or a non-ministerial department. A body delivering a service closely tied to ministerial policy is more likely to be an executive agency or part of a department. When answering a question about accountability, officials should be clear which form of body is involved, because the form determines who sets budgets, appoints leaders and answers for failures.

questions.prompt: A body needs to give independent expert advice on a technical subject but make no decisions. Which form is most suitable?

options.text: An executive agency, with a chief executive and a framework document
An advisory non-departmental public body
A ministerial department, led by a secretary of state in the usual way
A public corporation, which is independent and accountable to its own board

questions.hint: Advisory bodies give independent advice without making executive decisions.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an executive agency from an NDPB?

options.text: An executive agency has no chief executive, because the department's Permanent Secretary leads it
An NDPB is always larger than an executive agency and employs more staff in total
An executive agency is part of its parent department, while an NDPB works at arm's length from ministers
An executive agency can never deliver public services directly to the public

questions.hint: Agencies sit inside departments; NDPBs are arm's length.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a non-ministerial department is correct?

options.text: It has no accountability to Parliament, because it is independent of the government
It is led directly by the Prime Minister, who appoints its senior leaders
It is funded entirely by income from its own charges, so has no budget from the Treasury
It is not run day to day by a minister but is accountable to Parliament through one

questions.hint: Non-ministerial departments have no minister running them day to day.

questions.prompt: A new function needs strong independence from ministers, such as deciding appeals. Which form is the best fit?

options.text: A tribunal or other independent NDPB
A branch within a ministerial department
An executive agency reporting to the minister weekly
A team in the Cabinet Office

questions.hint: Independence suits a tribunal or similar body.

questions.prompt: Why does the form of a public body matter for accountability?

options.text: It determines how the body's logo and branding are approved by the department
It affects only the staff's pay scales and terms and conditions of work
It has no bearing on accountability, which is the same for every public body
It determines who sets budgets, appoints leaders and answers for failures

questions.hint: Form shapes lines of accountability.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of an executive agency?

options.text: The BBC, which is run by its own board and is independent of the department
A parliamentary select committee, which scrutinises the work of the department
The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency
A local council, which delivers services in its area under its own elected members

questions.hint: DVLA is an executive agency of the Department for Transport.

questions.prompt: A service is closely tied to ministers' policy and needs quick political direction. Which form is the best fit?

options.text: An executive agency or a part of the department
A tribunal NDPB, which is separate from the department and from ministers
An independent regulator, which sets its own priorities and makes its own decisions
A public corporation, with its own board and a high degree of independence

questions.hint: Close policy links point to departmental forms.

questions.prompt: Which body is most accurately described as a public corporation?

options.text: HM Revenue and Customs
The BBC
The Home Office
An advisory committee

questions.hint: Public corporations are largely independent, such as the BBC.

items.title: L11: The four accounting officer standards in practice
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money, chapter 3; Accounting Officer System Statements
items.body: An accounting officer is personally answerable to Parliament for how a department or body spends public money. Managing Public Money sets four standards that guide the accounting officer's advice and decisions. Regularity means spending complies with the legal authority Parliament has given and with the relevant rules, including Treasury rules. Propriety means that spending meets Parliament's high expectations of public conduct, including fairness, honesty, impartiality and avoiding waste and personal gain. Value for money means achieving the best mix of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, taking account of the quality of outcomes. Feasibility means that a proposal can be implemented successfully, with realistic assumptions, timelines, delivery capability and risks. In practice, an official preparing advice for the accounting officer should identify which standard a proposal puts at risk. For example, a payment made without legal authority raises a regularity issue. A contract awarded to a minister's friend without a fair process raises a propriety concern, even if legal. A scheme that costs far more than a cheaper alternative with the same results raises value for money. A programme with an impossible timeline and no delivery plan raises feasibility. The accounting officer may ask for a written direction if a minister proceeds against their advice on the standards. The standards apply to all spending, not only large projects, and they apply in difficult circumstances such as emergencies, though there may be more flexibility on how to meet them.

questions.prompt: A grant is paid to an organisation without the legal authority Parliament has granted. Which standard is most directly breached?

options.text: Value for money
Regularity
Feasibility
Propriety

questions.hint: Spending without legal authority is a regularity matter.

questions.prompt: A department awards a contract to a friend of a minister without competition, though no law is broken. Which standard is most directly in question?

options.text: Regularity
Feasibility
Value for money only
Propriety

questions.hint: Legal conduct can still fall short of Parliament's expectations of fairness.

questions.prompt: A programme has a delivery date that its own plan shows cannot be met. Which standard does this raise?

options.text: Regularity
Propriety
Feasibility
Economy only

questions.hint: Feasibility concerns whether it can be delivered.

questions.prompt: A scheme costs twice as much as an alternative that would achieve the same outcome. Which standard is most relevant?

options.text: Value for money
Regularity, because the cost is higher than it need be
Feasibility, because the scheme may not be achievable
Propriety, because the higher cost is unfair to taxpayers

questions.hint: Cost against outcomes is about value for money.

questions.prompt: What is the accounting officer's role in relation to the four standards?

options.text: To set the department's policy in the areas where it spends public money
To decide which of the standards ministers must follow when they take decisions
To advise on them and answer to Parliament for how public money is managed
To audit the department's accounts on behalf of Parliament each financial year

questions.hint: The accounting officer answers for spending against the standards.

questions.prompt: Which spending do the four accounting officer standards cover?

options.text: Only projects above a set cost threshold
Only capital spending, not day-to-day running costs
Only the first year of a new programme
All spending, whatever its size

questions.hint: The standards apply across spending.

questions.prompt: How do the standards apply in an emergency?

options.text: They are suspended until the emergency ends, when spending is reviewed afterwards
They still apply, but there may be flexibility in how they are met, with decisions recorded
They apply only to the Treasury, which has to approve all emergency spending
They apply only to procurement, so other spending is free from them during an emergency

questions.hint: Flexibility in method does not mean abandoning the standards.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a proper use of the standards by an official?

options.text: Identifying which standard a proposal puts at risk when preparing advice for the accounting officer
Using them to refuse any proposal that costs money, since public money must always be saved
Using them to decide the minister's policy, since the standards set out what policy should be
Using them only after the money is spent, when the department's accounts are prepared

questions.hint: They guide advice before decisions are taken.

items.title: L11: Meeting stakeholders and keeping a note
items.source: Ministerial Code; Civil Service Code; GOV.UK transparency publication of ministers' meetings with external organisations
items.body: Officials meet stakeholders such as charities, trade bodies, companies, unions and campaign groups as part of normal policy work. These meetings help the department to understand an issue and to test ideas. They also carry risks, so officials follow some sensible habits. Be clear who you represent and avoid giving a stakeholder privileged access or inside information that others do not have. Treat different groups fairly, and be willing to meet those with opposing views. Do not give a commitment about future policy or funding, because decisions belong to ministers and, for funding, to the proper process. Never accept anything of significant value from a stakeholder, and register and declare any hospitality or gift in line with the department's rules. Keep a note of who attended, what was discussed and any actions agreed. Where the discussion concerns a commercial or sensitive matter, take care over confidential information, and consider whether a conflict of interest arises. Departments publish, usually every quarter, information on ministers' external meetings, gifts and hospitality and overseas travel, and senior officials' meetings may also be published, so officials should be able to explain why each meeting took place. If a stakeholder asks for confidential information, an official should say what can and cannot be shared and, if needed, refer the request to the right team, such as the FOI team. If a lobbying approach seems to cross a line, the official should report it to their line manager.

questions.prompt: At a meeting a trade body asks whether funding will be renewed next year. The decision has not been made. What should the official say?

options.text: That renewal is very likely, so that the trade body can plan its own budget with confidence
That it depends on how far the body supports the minister's policy in the coming months
That the decision has not been made and will be taken through the proper process
That funding is guaranteed for the next two years, because it has always been renewed before

questions.hint: Officials do not pre-empt decisions that belong elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why should an official be willing to meet groups on both sides of a contested issue?

options.text: The Code requires equal numbers of meetings with each side of every debate
To treat stakeholders fairly and to test ideas against different views
It is the only way to avoid having the meetings published by the department
Each side can then be told what the other said, so that the dispute is resolved sooner

questions.hint: Fair access supports impartiality and better policy.

questions.prompt: A company representative offers a high-value hospitality package after a meeting. What is the correct response?

options.text: Decline it, or declare it under the department's rules if it cannot be refused politely
Accept it, as it is meant as a courtesy and refusing might harm the relationship
Accept it and say nothing, since it was not a gift but part of an ordinary business meeting
Accept it and arrange a return favour, so that the relationship stays on an even footing

questions.hint: Offers of significant value should be declined or declared.

questions.prompt: Which entry belongs in a meeting note?

options.text: The attendees' private opinions of each other, to help the minister prepare for later meetings
A full transcript of every word spoken, so that nothing can be disputed later
The official's guesses about how the minister will decide, so the team can plan ahead
Who attended, the main points discussed and actions agreed

questions.hint: A note should be factual and useful.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the quarterly publication of ministers' external meetings?

options.text: To tell stakeholders what the minister thinks about each issue discussed
To list the department's staff and show who works on which policy area
To make government contact with outside organisations open to scrutiny
To replace the need for Freedom of Information requests about ministers' meetings

questions.hint: Transparency about meetings supports public trust.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks to see a draft of unpublished policy. What is the proper response?

options.text: Decline, since early access gives an unfair advantage and the policy is not yet for release
Share it informally, as the stakeholder is supportive and has helped with the policy
Share it if the stakeholder promises to keep it private until it has been published
Share the parts that are not controversial, and hold back the rest until the decision is made

questions.hint: Giving privileged access undermines fairness.

questions.prompt: How should an official respond to a lobbying approach that seems improper?

options.text: Ignore it, as lobbying is always legitimate
Ask the lobbyist to write to the minister instead
Delete any record of it
Report it to their line manager

questions.hint: Concerns about an improper approach should be raised.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for commercially sensitive information about another company. What should the official do?

options.text: Pass it on, because it supports the aims of the policy and will help the stakeholder
Explain it cannot be shared and refer any formal request to the right team
Share only a summary of it, to show goodwill without giving away the detail
Tell the stakeholder to ask the other company directly for permission to share it

questions.hint: Commercial confidentiality is respected unless a proper process applies.
